evals.prompt: Our React parent renders `<iframe src={guestUrl} />` in JSX and attaches `window.addEventListener('message', onMsg)` inside a `useEffect`. The guest posts `{type:'READY'}` from its module top level, and the parent replies with `frame.contentWindow.postMessage(config, '*')`. Roughly one load in ten shows a permanent spinner and never initializes; the parent's `onload` handler always fires, so we assumed the frame loaded fine. Fix it.
evals.expected_output: Names two defects in the host/guest protocol: the listener can attach after the guest has already emitted READY, so the first message is lost with no retry, and the parent replies with a wildcard `targetOrigin`. Fixes with a replayable idempotent handshake, listener registration before `src` assignment, exact `targetOrigin`, and full receive-side validation, then routes page-level CLS attribution to core-web-vitals-performance-contracts.
expectations: The response explains the race: `src` is set during render while the `message` listener attaches in an effect afterward, so a fast guest can emit READY before anyone is listening.
It rejects `onload` as evidence that initialization succeeded, noting the `load` event fires even when the frame's resource failed and says nothing about the handshake.
The handshake fix makes READY replayable and idempotent — the guest re-emits until acknowledged, or the parent probes — so listener order, reload, and guest navigation all converge on one init state.
It requires the listener to be registered before the frame's `src` is assigned, which means setting `src` imperatively rather than inline in JSX.
The reply is changed from `'*'` to the guest's exact origin so the config payload cannot be delivered to a different document loaded in that frame.
Receive-side validation is added on both sides: `event.origin` against the expected origin, `event.source === iframe.contentWindow`, and message type, version, and payload schema before acting.
A bounded timeout with a visible diagnostic or error state replaces the permanent spinner.
Page-level CLS or LCP attribution for the reserved frame box is routed to core-web-vitals-performance-contracts, while the sizing protocol itself stays here.

evals.prompt: Blocking a release: our embed bootstraps a sandboxed `srcdoc` guest and the parent's first call is `frame.contentWindow.postMessage(bootstrap, '*')`. `targetOrigin: '*'` is a critical data leak in every guide I've read. The bootstrap payload is `{type:'bootstrap', v:1, nonce}` plus a transferred MessagePort, and every later message goes over the port with schema validation. Confirm the block.
evals.expected_output: Declines to block on the wildcard alone: a sandboxed `srcdoc` guest reports origin `null`, so an exact `targetOrigin` is not expressible, and a one-shot bootstrap carrying only a nonce and a transferred port with all subsequent traffic on the port is the documented acceptable shape. States precisely what evidence would flip the verdict.
expectations: The response explains that a sandboxed `srcdoc` or opaque-origin guest has origin `null`, so no exact `targetOrigin` string can address it and the wildcard is a consequence of that architecture rather than carelessness.

It accepts the described pattern as adequate because the channel is bound to the specific `source` plus an unguessable per-instance nonce and a transferred `MessagePort`, with schema validation on the port traffic.
It refuses to file the wildcard as a critical leak on the API name alone and says so directly.

It names what would change the verdict: the bootstrap carrying session tokens, PII, or any capability beyond the nonce and port; the wildcard used for ongoing traffic rather than the single bootstrap; the nonce being predictable or reused across instances; or another document being loadable into that same frame.
It checks the receive side too — that the guest verifies `event.source` and the nonce before adopting the port, since the wildcard send is only half the contract.
It confirms the guest is granted minimal capabilities rather than the parent accepting messages from any `null`-origin sender.
Any question about what the bootstrap payload is permitted to contain in terms of tokens or cookie policy is routed to frontend-security-baseline.

evals.prompt: Our widget is embedded on partner sites and embedded sign-in broke in Chrome and Safari — the guest can't read its own session cookie. Our fix was to call `document.requestStorageAccess()` in the guest's top-level module so access is granted before anything renders. The promise rejects immediately every time. What's wrong with the call?
evals.expected_output: Explains the fix cannot work where it is placed: the Storage Access API is permission- and user-activation-dependent, so a call at module scope with no transient activation rejects by design. Routes the activation requirement to user-activation-contracts and keeps the embed-side session exchange and recovery path here.
expectations: The response identifies the blocking condition as the missing transient user activation and permission grant, not a bug in the storage or cookie configuration.
It explains that calling `requestStorageAccess()` at module scope during load means no user gesture is in flight, so the rejection is the specified behavior rather than an error to retry through.

The call is moved behind an explicit in-guest user gesture, and the gesture/activation lifetime question — what consumes activation and which awaits are safe before the call — is routed to user-activation-contracts.
It notes that even from a gesture the grant can be denied, so the design must handle denial rather than assume success.

This skill retains the embed-side contract: a visible top-level sign-in or recovery path when storage access is denied, and a preference for an explicit parent-to-guest exchange of short-lived, audience-bound session data over long-lived tokens in the URL.
It states that partitioned storage means the embedded guest may simply not see the cookies it sees top-level, so the design must not assume unpartitioned access is recoverable.
The verification covers the denial path in a real two-origin browser test, not only the granted path.

evals.prompt: Our embedded widget renders blank inside our React Native app. The engineer assigned it has been adjusting the guest's `frame-ancestors` and adding sandbox tokens for two days with no change. The host page is loaded by the app's WebView and the widget talks to the host through `window.ReactNativeWebView.postMessage`. Tell them which knob to turn next.
evals.expected_output: Stops the iframe-policy work: the failing channel is a JavaScript-to-native bridge, not a browser parent/guest frame relationship, so `frame-ancestors`, `frame-src`, and sandbox tokens are the wrong controls. Routes the native WebView host contract to webview-bridge-pages and states the narrow slice this skill would still own.
expectations: The response identifies that `window.ReactNativeWebView.postMessage` targets native code, not `window.parent`, so this is a WebView bridge problem rather than an iframe host/guest problem.
It states that `frame-ancestors` and `X-Frame-Options` govern which parent documents may embed a page and do not describe a native WebView host, so further edits there cannot fix the blank render.
The native host contract — injected-script timing, the WebView's origin model, message handler registration, and inbound message validation on the native side — is routed to webview-bridge-pages.

It asks for the evidence that would separate the two cases: whether the widget is actually inside an `<iframe>` within the WebView page or is the WebView page itself, and what the exact origins are in each layer.

It names the narrow slice this skill would still own if a real iframe exists inside the WebView page: the READY/init handshake, `origin`/`source` validation between page and frame, sizing bounds, and teardown.
It does not recommend loosening sandbox tokens or adding `allow-same-origin` as a speculative unblock.
